text.p: Britain's fledgling Internet advertising market is expected to grow exponentially this year, fuelled by a growing stable of Internet advertising sales houses.

"We see this market growing to about six million pounds ($9.6 million) this year," Carol Dukes, a director of EMAP Online, told Reuters in a phone interview. EMAP Online, part of British media group EMAP Plc, recently launched EMAP Internet Sales, a sales house for Web site advertising.

EMAP Online estimates the UK advertising market on the Internet's World Wide Web in 1996 was about one million to 1.5 million pounds. Some estimates have put the figure as high as four million pounds. In 1995, just one year earlier, the Internet advertising market in the UK was almost non-existent.

EMAP projects advertising for UK-based Web sites will reach 80 million pounds in 2000. By comparison, commercial radio in Britain currently generates ad revenues of about 400 million pounds a year -- and is a small player in the country's media market.

EMAP Internet Sales is but one of several Internet sales houses to be established in the UK. TSMS, the television sales house owned by Britain's United News & Media Plc, in February formed a division for new media sales, including selling advertising on the Internet and on CD-ROMs.

Other players include the Electronic Telegraph, the Web site version of the Daily Telegraph which earlier this month said it would sell advertising space on other Web sites as well as its own, and Softbank.
"Advertisers still have a great deal of trouble buying space," EMAP's Dukes said. "There are so many Web sites and they are very small. We are trying to provide a one-stop shop."
The need is clearly felt from the advertisers' side.

"Because there are so many new things coming out it's quite a complex job to know what's going on," Jane Ostler, digital communications planner at the Network, the new media arm of advertising agency Ogilvy & Mather, told Reuters.
"In the print market, in the TV market you know what's going on," Ostler added. "So the formation of sales houses is a good thing, and hopefully it will make the process easier for us."
Internet sales houses are typically patterned after television sales houses, packaging together Web sites with similar audiences for sale to advertisers.

Web Site advertising in the UK remains a narrow market, and advertisers tend to focus on the Web's predominantly male audience. Ogilvy & Mather's Ostler said UK-based Web sites continue to be dominated by adverts for software, computers and automotive products.
The Internet, however, has potential for advertising that extends well beyond the banner advertising being sold by Internet sales houses.

"We are looking at other new models, things like sponsorship, promotions and competition opportunities -- areas of even joint content development and sponsorship of Webcasts, which wouldn't normally fit into a standard advertising model," Ostler said.
The Internet's multi-media format combined with an ability to target very specific audiences means it offers unique opportunities to advertisers.

"Advertising on the Web can bring us one-to-one communication," said Danny Meadows-Klue, product manager for the Electronic Telegraph. "It can be like market research. In a way it can be like radio. In a way it can be like television."
"It is not a medium," Dukes said. "It is an environment. Many of the businesses on the Web are shops."

Consumer purchases from Web sites remain limited, in part because credit cards -- the only payment mechanism now available on the Internet -- are not economically feasible for purchases under 10 pounds.
"I think we'll see a little bit of a change when micropayments become possible," said Dukes. "There's things that you might might to pay 10 pence for that you might not pay 10 pounds for."
